b: tl;dr: the Explorer Pattern is one individual or team building a functional implementation that minimizes cross-team and cross-functional impacts as much as humanly possible, and then reconciling the details with other teams after that prototype is completed, accepting that this approach can require very substantial rework to that initial development.

Imprint previously called this the “Tech-led” or “Engineering-led” development model, but it’s pretty unclear to folks what that means. This writeup provides a more defined term, the “Explorer Pattern”, and explains in more detail how this works.
Why do we need to adjust the way we work?
Code is expensive, and we design process to minimize implementation and rework

Writing software is extremely cheap, but it’s a wider phenomenon: generating output is effectively-free across many dimensions. Code is nearly free — if we have appropriate constraints. Designs are nearly free — if they follow patterns. Analysis is nearly free — if we’ve instrumented things properly

Reworking software is extremely cheap. Historically industry has optimized around avoiding engineering rework because engineering was the highest cost / narrowest constraint. In many companies this was interpreted as writing code being the constraint, which was never true, but many common practices were designed as if that were true (e.g. bringing engineering into problem-solving late “to protect their time”)

Working on the system is much more effective than historically if we get automated integration and feedback loops right, e.g. not improving a one-off design but improving the design system. Any place where improving the higher-leverage process is slower than solving the one-off is a bug in our process

The easiest metaphor to think about the Explorer Pattern is database replication. Databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL have a primary database, where writes are performed. Every write is verified at that point, and once it’s verified, you know that the writes will flow downstream to various secondary replicas. Those downstream replicas can be delayed but they can’t be wrong because writes are verified upstream. (I’ve resisted the desire to talk about the CAP theorem.)

A different model for database design is that used by Dynamo or Cassandra (or MongoDB to a certain extent), where you have a replica set, and have to get an acknowledgement from the majority of the replica set for a write to be strongly consistent. This is a very reliable setup, because it means you can tolerate losing a node, but it also introduces inconsistencies, and on a fixed amount of hardware they tend to be much, much slower than running a primary-secondary setup (or rely on bad performance metrics that don’t fsync to disk to create the illusion of throughput).

The Explorer Pattern is the former primary-secondary model, where the vast majority of the work is done by the working individual or team. This makes all work internally consistent because it’s passed through the same small group. It doesn’t, however, mean that the work is perfect. For example, you can always insert data that meets the table’s requirements but is still inherently wrong (e.g. 200 is a valid integer, but it doesn’t mean that my credit limit was supposed to be 200, that depends on the surrounding application logic).

Other teams become aware of the changes downstream, not synchronously upfront, and it’s instead the working group’s responsibility to both rationalize approach and create visibility into their work for other teams to engage in a non-blocking fashion.

A concrete example of this practice at Imprint was rolling out financial aggregator support, e.g. allowing folks to connect to their Imprint powered accounts via Plaid.
This has always been something folks want, but it’s particularly important in the realm of agentic commerce where more folks’ agents are analyzing their financial
state for them. For this project, one of our engineering leaders (Ron), built the first pass of the feature at a low-burn while understanding the shape of the problem
in a private alpha. He chatted through some of the details periodically to keep other teams aware,
but it was a bit of a side project.

However, once he found the full shape of the problem and had implemented a full solution, we cut the replica-lag across teams down to near-zero,
identified and ran through the small number of remaining issues, and shipped it. Like many of our projects this year, it was never officially
on a roadmap, and shipped a quality feature that our members have wanted for some time.
How to follow the Explorer pattern
The rough rules for following the Explorer pattern:

Know your goal and sponsor: every initiative ultimately has to have a specific outcome it’s pursuing and a sponsor who’s bankrolling that pursuit. This doesn’t always need to be explicit, especially for smaller projects, but once a project goes beyond ~3 weeks of effort, if you can’t very explicitly identify who the stakeholder is sponsoring your project and they would not enthusiastically agree, then you are likely closer to “lost” than “exploring”
Small working group is small: at most 5 people, and preferably smaller. Everyone in the group has to keep the entire project in their head for as long as possible to detect problems and opportunities

Small working group is flexible: folks in small working groups have to “find a way to yes” rather than “find a way to no”. Exploring is about uncovering the fundamental shape of a problem rather than pretending we know the fundamental shape
Publish progress in a public channel: explorers have to report home with the progress they are making so others are aware. This is both a Linear Project and a Slack channel.

Make the narrowest viable changes to what already exists: when we introduce unnecessary changes, we invalidate others’ mental models about how the world works. When we haven’t made those changes with care, we’re not only invalidating others’ mental model, we are creating the expectation that we’ve done it very intentionally for a good reason, which has a chilling effect on others improving them later, which is very expensive, whereas the Explorer pattern depends on being as inexpensive as possible

Exercise good judgment to identify reasonable hypotheses: discard bad ideas immediately, and then filter the rest by trying to implement them as quickly as possible. Once you see the shape of the implementation, you can figure out which of the remainders are interesting

Hold assumptions constant to avoid getting stuck: the only way to navigate complex ambiguous problems is to hold things constant, even when you know they are imperfect. For example, to do headcount planning we have to know our revenue, to know our revenue we have to forecast it, to forecast it we have to know the day that partners will go live next year. We don’t truly know any of those things, so just anchoring on a plausible guess to unblock us is much more valuable than trying to get them accurate. A little prework is useful, but a lot is just artificial precision that’s a distraction from progress

Hold space for being totally wrong: when we move fast, with low information, we always find the way out, but often it’s not the way out we anticipated when we got started. Being open to throwing it all away, and starting a second, third, fourth time

Ship all the way to production behind a feature flag: features and products move fast when we get the pieces working every step from frontend to backend to data pulls. This is the first step of exploration. Just make sure it’s behind a feature flag that’s only enabled for internal folks!
